summary: The XRD data across the paper demonstrate the formation and structural evolution of CsPbBr3-based nanocrystals and heterostructures, with clear evidence for phase purity, crystallinity improvements with processing, and successful integration with other materials (such as g-C3N4 and SiO2 matrices). The results show consistent trends in peak sharpening and intensity with reaction time or composite formation, and reveal the coexistence of multiple phases in heterostructures.
experimental_variables: sample composition (pure CsPbBr3, perovskite QDs, g-C3N4 variants, heterostructures)

key_findings.finding: CsPbBr3 nanocrystals synthesized via microwave-assisted methods show increasing XRD peak intensity and sharpening with longer reaction times, indicating improved crystallinity and possible grain growth.
Bulk perovskite QDs exhibit sharp, well-defined XRD peaks distinct from those of CsPbBr3 nanocrystals, suggesting high crystallinity and phase purity.

S-g-C3N4 (USCN), SCN, and CN samples display broad peaks at ~13.1° and ~27.5°, while CPB and CPB/USCN heterostructures show additional sharp peaks, indicating the presence of crystalline CsPbBr3 alongside the g-C3N4 matrix.

H-CPB composites (CsPbBr3 embedded in CsPb2Br5/SiO2) show additional XRD peaks compared to pure SiO2, with peak intensity increasing from H-CPB (1) to H-CPB (3), indicating successful incorporation and increasing crystallinity or phase fraction of perovskite phases.

Across heterostructure samples (fig_29, fig_30), the XRD patterns consistently show the coexistence of perovskite and host/matrix phases, with no evidence of significant phase decomposition or impurity formation.

scientific_interpretation: The combined XRD results indicate that CsPbBr3 nanocrystals and quantum dots can be synthesized with high crystallinity, as evidenced by sharp, intense peaks (fig_11, fig_13). Reaction time is a key variable for optimizing crystallinity in microwave-assisted synthesis (fig_11). When CsPbBr3 is incorporated into heterostructures with g-C3N4 (fig_29) or embedded in CsPb2Br5/SiO2 matrices (fig_30), the XRD patterns reveal the retention of perovskite crystallinity alongside the host material, suggesting that the heterostructure formation does not disrupt the perovskite phase. The additional peaks in heterostructure samples (fig_29, fig_30) compared to pure host materials confirm successful integration and phase coexistence. The trend of increasing peak intensity in H-CPB composites (fig_30) may reflect higher perovskite content or improved ordering. There is no evidence from the XRD data of major phase impurities or decomposition products in any of the heterostructures studied.
limitations: Phase assignments are not explicitly provided for all peaks; identification relies on comparison to reference patterns mentioned in captions.
Quantitative phase fractions, crystallite sizes, and lattice parameters are not reported.
Peak intensity and width trends are described qualitatively; no numerical FWHM or intensity ratios are given.
The relationship between XRD features and functional properties (e.g., photocatalytic activity) is not directly established from the XRD data alone.
Possible minor impurity phases or amorphous content cannot be ruled out without more detailed analysis.
